stages.title: 3 · Learn instead of count
stages.goal: Train bigram logits by gradient descent and record loss.
stages.lesson: Softmax converts scores to probabilities. Cross entropy is minus the log probability assigned to the observed next token. import numpy as np
def train(ids: list[int], size: int, steps: int = 80, lr: float = 0.5) -> tuple[np.ndarray, list[float]]:
    if len(ids)<2: raise ValueError('Need two tokens')
    x=np.asarray(ids[:-1]); y=np.asarray(ids[1:]); w=np.zeros((size,size)); history=[]
    for step in range(steps+1):
        z=w[x]; p=np.exp(z-z.max(1,keepdims=True)); p/=p.sum(1,keepdims=True)
        history.append(float(-np.log(p[np.arange(len(y)),y]).mean()))
        if step==steps: break
        g=p.copy(); g[np.arange(len(y)),y]-=1; grad=np.zeros_like(w)
        np.add.at(grad,x,g/len(y)); w-=lr*grad
    return w,history

import numpy as np
def train_mlp(x: np.ndarray, y: list[int], classes: int, steps: int = 250, lr: float = 0.3) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, list[float]]:
    x=np.asarray(x,dtype=float); y=np.asarray(y); rng=np.random.default_rng(7)
    a=rng.normal(0,0.2,(x.shape[1],12)); b=rng.normal(0,0.2,(12,classes)); losses=[]
    for i in range(steps+1):
        h=np.tanh(x@a); z=h@b; p=np.exp(z-z.max(1,keepdims=True)); p/=p.sum(1,keepdims=True)
        losses.append(float(-np.log(p[np.arange(len(y)),y]).mean()))
        if i==steps: break
        dz=p.copy(); dz[np.arange(len(y)),y]-=1; dz/=len(y)
        da=x.T@((dz@b.T)*(1-h*h)); db=h.T@dz
        a-=lr*da; b-=lr*db
    return a,b,losses

stages.title: 5 · Look back with attention
stages.goal: Implement scaled, causal self-attention.
stages.lesson: Queries ask what a position needs; keys describe what earlier positions offer; values carry the information. Scores are QKᵀ divided by the square root of key width. import numpy as np
def attention(q: np.ndarray, k: np.ndarray, v: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    scores=q@k.T/np.sqrt(q.shape[-1]); mask=np.triu(np.ones(scores.shape,dtype=bool),1)
    scores=np.where(mask,-np.inf,scores); weights=np.exp(scores-scores.max(1,keepdims=True))
    weights/=weights.sum(1,keepdims=True)
    return weights@v,weights

stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Python functions, lists, dictionaries, slicing, loops, exceptions. No gradients or neural-network knowledge required.

Python on iPad remains on HOLD. These are authored lessons and optional reference sources, not a claim that your code has run. Use an explicitly chosen local host CLI for real checks. No notes, credentials or downloaded corpus are needed: start with synthetic text you can inspect.

A model is learned from training text. Development text helps choose settings; test text measures the frozen choice. Split before learning an alphabet. If you build the vocabulary from the whole text, you have let future evaluation data change your model. A character tokenizer is a list of symbols plus a dictionary mapping each symbol to an integer. Sorting makes IDs reproducible; spaces and newlines are symbols, not cleanup. Reserve <UNK> at index0. In replace mode, map a new character to0 without changing the vocabulary. In error mode, reject it clearly. Decoding an unknown produces the visible marker <UNK>, so only known text promises an exact round trip.

Explain why letting the helicopter add a new vocabulary slot leaks evaluation information. Independent milestone: handle a new Unicode/whitespace example from the checks without adding symbols. Skills are taught here; there is no assumed prior AI expertise.

stages.title: 2 · Count directed, overlapping transitions
stages.goal: Build and explain a row-normalized add-k transition matrix.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Python indexing/loops and ValueError; stage1 training-only vocabulary; 2D NumPy shapes, conditional probability and fractions.

Rows mean current token; columns mean next token. Every adjacent pair counts, including overlapping pairs. Add k to each cell, then divide each row by its own total: P[j|i]=(C[i,j]+k)/(sum_j C[i,j]+kV). For k>0 every in-vocabulary next token has positive probability. This does not imply a lower held-out loss than uniform. With k=0 an entirely unseen row uses an explicit uniform fallback; an unseen transition in a seen row can still have probability zero. Unknown characters are handled by the tokenizer policy, not by growing V here.

Counterexample: [0,0,1] produces a uniform matrix, so transposing its probabilities reveals nothing. For [0,1,1], both rows are [1/3,2/3], not [1/4,3/4] in the second row. We need several asymmetric fixtures and unequal row totals to diagnose orientation and broadcasting.

Guided activity A: draw counts for [0,0,0,1,1,0] and mark five adjacent arrows. Guided activity B: add a third, unseen symbol and compare its prior-only row with rows that have observations. Keep exact fractions until the final decimal display.

stages.title: 3 · Measure surprise on held-out transitions
stages.goal: Implement cross-entropy, perplexity and two honest baselines.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Stages1–2; natural logarithm and exp; arithmetic mean; probabilities sum to one. The lesson supplies a hand calculation before code.

A next-token probability is judged on an observed transition. Surprise in natural-log units (nats) is -ln(p). Cross-entropy is the mean over N=len(ids)-1 transitions, not the number of characters. Perplexity exp(loss) translates that mean back into an effective number of choices. A uniform V-token baseline has loss ln(V) and perplexity V. A unigram baseline counts training token frequencies, adds k and repeats that same next-token distribution for every current token; it ignores order.

Do not score the same pairs used to fit and call that held-out performance. A zero-probability observed transition has infinite loss; silently adding epsilon changes the reported model. For positive k, in-vocabulary transitions have nonzero probability, but smoothing does not guarantee a win over uniform. An unobserved context at k=0 uses the explicitly stated uniform fallback; a missing transition from an observed context can still give infinite loss. Unknown characters must already be mapped by stage1.

Guided activity A: compute a two-transition loss from probabilities1/2 and1/4: -(ln(1/2)+ln(1/4))/2≈1.03972 nats and perplexity≈2.82843. Guided activity B: find a held-out transition where a skewed training model loses to uniform, then explain why this does not make the measurement wrong. stages.title: 1 · Tokens from merges (byte-pair encoding)
stages.goal: Learn BPE merges from training text, encode new text with them in order, and decode losslessly.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Python lists, dicts, tuples and while-loops. Recommended first: tinylm2 stage 1 (training-only vocabulary).

A model never sees letters, only token ids. Characters give a tiny vocabulary but long sequences; whole words give short sequences but an endless vocabulary, and any new word is unknown. Byte-pair encoding (BPE) sits between them. Start from characters, then repeatedly find the most frequent adjacent pair and glue it into one new symbol. Each glue step is a merge, and the ordered list of merges is the tokenizer.

Three rules make it deterministic and testable:
1. Count every adjacent pair, overlapping ones included: “aaaa” has the pair (a,a) three times.
2. When merging, scan left to right and never reuse a symbol: “aaaa” becomes [aa, aa], not [aa, a, a] or [a, aa, a].
3. Ties go to the smallest pair in Python's tuple order, so two runs always agree. Stop early when no pair occurs at least twice, because a merge seen once only memorises.

Encoding new text replays the learned merges in the order they were learned, not by frequency in the new text. Decoding is joining the strings, and because every merge only concatenates, decode(encode(x)) == x for any text, even characters never seen in training. Those stay single-character tokens. That losslessness is BPE's advantage over an <UNK> token.

Misconception: “the merge count is the vocabulary size.” Not quite: the vocabulary is the training characters plus one new symbol per merge, and you may get fewer merges than you asked for.
Counterexample: in “aaaa” the pair count (3) is not the number of tokens a merge produces (2). If you test only on text without repeated letters, an overlapping-merge bug never shows.

Real tokenizers such as GPT-2's run BPE on bytes and split on spaces first. This stage keeps spaces as ordinary symbols, so merges can cross word boundaries. Say so in your README.

stages.title: 2 · Scores, softmax and loss
stages.goal: Turn raw scores (logits) into probabilities stably and measure them with cross-entropy.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Stage 1; NumPy arrays and axis=; exp and natural log. Recommended: tinylm2 stage 3 (held-out loss).

A neural language model doesn't output probabilities directly. For each position it outputs one raw score per vocabulary token, called logits. Softmax turns a row of logits z into probabilities: p_i = exp(z_i) / Σ_j exp(z_j). Bigger score, bigger share; every share is positive; the row sums to 1.

Two facts you will use constantly:
1. Softmax ignores adding the same constant to every logit in a row. So subtract the row's maximum before exp. The result is identical, and exp never sees a huge number. Without this, logits like [1000, 999] overflow to inf/inf = nan.
2. Cross-entropy is the average of −ln p(target) over positions, measured in nats. A model that knows nothing (all logits equal) scores ln V. With V=3 that is ln 3 ≈ 1.0986. This is your first baseline: any trained model should beat ln V on held-out text, or it has learned nothing.

Compute cross-entropy straight from logits with log-softmax: log p = (z − max) − ln Σ exp(z − max). Computing softmax and then log is mathematically the same but loses precision when a probability underflows to 0.

Misconception: “softmax along any axis is fine.” Rows are positions and columns are vocabulary entries. Normalising down a column mixes different positions' predictions.
Counterexample: [[2,1,0],[0,0,5]] normalised by column gives a first row that doesn't sum to 1.

Guided activity A: by hand, softmax [2,1,0] ≈ [0.665, 0.245, 0.090]; the loss for target 0 is −ln 0.665 ≈ 0.408, and for target 2 it is ≈ 2.408. Guided activity B: predict what happens to softmax([1000, 999]) in a naive implementation, then in yours.

Prerequisites: Stage 2; derivatives of exp and ln; the chain rule; matrix indexing.

In tinylm2 you counted transitions. Now the same model is learned the way every neural network is: a table W of logits (row = current token, column = next token), a loss, and repeated small steps downhill.

The one derivative to know: for one position with probabilities p = softmax(z) and target y, ∂loss/∂z = p − onehot(y). Derivation: loss = −z_y + ln Σ exp(z_j). The derivative of ln Σ exp(z_j) with respect to z_i is p_i, and −z_y contributes −1 at i = y. For a mean over N positions, divide by N.
Each position's gradient lands on the row of W for that position's current token, so rows used several times add up. That needs np.add.at, not plain assignment.

Before trusting any hand-written gradient, check it numerically: nudge one entry by ±ε, recompute the loss, and compare (L(w+ε) − L(w−ε)) / 2ε with your gradient. This finite-difference check is how you catch a missing /N or a wrong sign.

What training discovers: with zero initial weights and enough steps, each observed row's softmax approaches that row's transition frequencies, the same answer as counting with k=0. A row whose token never appears as a current token gets zero gradient forever, so it stays exactly uniform. Smoothing in counts and initialisation in learning both decide what unseen contexts look like.

Misconception: “lower training loss always means a better model.” This model can only reach the training frequencies, and on held-out text an over-confident row can lose to uniform (see tinylm2's counterexample).

stages.title: 4 · More context: embeddings and a hidden layer
stages.goal: Predict from the previous two tokens with learned embeddings and a tanh hidden layer, verified by gradient checks.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Stage 3; matrix multiplication shapes; tanh and its derivative 1 − tanh².

A bigram sees one token. In “1 2 3 4 2 5” repeated, the token after 2 is 3 if the token before was 1, and 5 if it was 4. No bigram can know which. Its best held-out loss stays stuck above zero, because both transitions out of 2 look the same to it.

Give the model a context of the previous `block` tokens:
1. make_contexts pads the start with token 0 and returns, for each position, the block tokens before it and the target at it. The target is never part of its own context. Including it is the classic off-by-one that makes training look perfect.
2. Embeddings: each token id indexes a learned row of E (V × d). The context's rows are concatenated into one vector of length block·d.
3. Hidden layer: h = tanh(flat·W1 + b1). Logits: h·W2 + b2. The loss is your stage-2 cross-entropy.

Backpropagation is the chain rule applied in reverse, and the shapes tell you each product:
d_logits = (softmax − onehot)/N; dW2 = hᵀ·d_logits; db2 = Σ rows; dh = d_logits·W2ᵀ; dpre = dh ⊙ (1 − h²); dW1 = flatᵀ·dpre; db1 = Σ rows; d_flat = dpre·W1ᵀ. Reshape d_flat back to (N, block, d) and scatter-add it into dE with np.add.at, because a token can appear in many contexts, and twice in one context.

Gradient-check every parameter with finite differences before training. The two classic bugs are using 1 − h instead of 1 − h², and losing repeated embedding gradients; both show up immediately.

Misconception: “a bigger model is always better.” A block-1 MLP on this data is no better than a bigram: dev loss ≈ 0.23 vs 0.26. Only the extra context helps (block 2: ≈ 0.003). Capacity without the right information doesn't help.

stages.title: 5 · Look back with causal self-attention
stages.goal: Implement single-head scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask, and verify what it can and cannot see.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Stages 2–4; dot products; matrix transpose; the stage-2 softmax.

The MLP has a fixed window and a separate weight for every slot in it. Attention lets every position decide how much to read from each earlier position, based on content.

For a sequence x (n × d), project three ways: queries Q = xWq (what am I looking for?), keys K = xWk (what do I offer?) and values V = xWv (what do I pass on?). Position i scores position j by Q_i·K_j / √d_k. Dividing by √d_k keeps scores from growing with the width, which would push softmax towards a single one-hot spike and tiny gradients. Each row of scores goes through your softmax, and the output is weights·V: a weighted average of earlier values.

A language model must not peek at the future when predicting the next token. So before the softmax, set every score where j > i to −∞. Those weights become exactly 0, and each row still sums to 1. Masking after the softmax (multiplying by 0) is wrong: rows no longer sum to 1, so outputs shrink for early positions.

Two consequences you can test:
1. Causality: changing token 2 must not change outputs 0 or 1.
2. No order inside the past: attention alone treats the earlier tokens as a set. Swapping x₀ and x₁ leaves output 2 unchanged. This is why stage 6 adds position embeddings.

Misconception: “attention weights explain the model.” They show where a position read from in this layer, not why the prediction came out as it did. Treat them as a diagnostic, not an explanation.

stages.title: 6 · Assemble a tiny transformer and sample
stages.goal: Build a pre-norm transformer block with positions, a seeded sampler with temperature and top-k, and fit its readout.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Stages 1–5; mean and variance; random number generators with seeds.

A transformer block is stage 5 plus three engineering ideas that make deep stacks trainable:
1. Positions: add a learned position vector to each token embedding, x = tok[ids] + pos[0:n]. Stage 5 showed attention can't see order otherwise.
2. Residual connections: x = x + attention(…) and then x = x + mlp(…). Each sub-layer adds a correction to a running stream instead of replacing it, so a block whose weights are zero is exactly the identity.
3. Layer normalisation (pre-norm): each sub-layer reads layer_norm(x), so every position's vector has mean 0 and variance 1 before entering. This keeps scales stable when blocks stack.
A final layer_norm, then a head matrix, gives logits for every position. Position t's logits must depend only on tokens 0…t; the causal mask makes the whole stack obey this, and a test checks it.

Generation is a loop: run the model on the last `context` ids, take the last row of logits, pick a next id and append it. Picking rules:
- temperature T divides the logits. T → 0 means always take the argmax (greedy, define T = 0 as exactly that); T = 1 is the model's distribution; T > 1 flattens it.
- top-k keeps only the k largest logits before the softmax (ties broken by lower id), so unlikely tokens can never appear.
- Use np.random.default_rng(seed) and pass it through, so the same seed in the same environment repeats exactly. A seed is not a promise across library versions.

Shapes and initialisation (the checks don't depend on your init, but the worked numbers do): with vocabulary V, context C, width d and hidden h, tok is V×d and pos is C×d, both drawn from normal(0, 0.5). wq, wk, wv and wo are d×d, w1 is d×h and head is d×V, all from normal(0, 1/√d). w2 is h×d from normal(0, 1/√h). Draw them in that order from np.random.default_rng(seed). A zero head is also a fine start, since only the head is trained here.

Honest scope for this stage: training every weight needs backpropagation through attention and layer norm, which is a stretch goal (and a natural use for PyTorch on your laptop, written by you). Here you train only the head on frozen transformer features, with your stage-3 gradient, to see the loss move. Record that clearly in your model card: “readout-only training on random features” is not a trained GPT.

Misconception: “a fluent sample proves the model is good.” Report held-out loss against the uniform (ln V) and bigram baselines, and show a sample as illustration only.

stages.title: 1 · Tokenize and parse a command line yourself
stages.goal: Write a quote-aware tokenizer and a parser for pipelines and redirects, with no shlex.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Python strings, indexing, while-loops, exceptions. Terminal Lab missions (quotes, pipes, > and >>) recommended.

Before a shell runs anything it turns one line of text into words and operators. Get this wrong and the right program runs with the wrong arguments, which is how both bugs and security holes start. Write it yourself as a small state machine that reads one character at a time:
- Outside quotes, space/tab/newline ends a word. `|`, `<`, `>` and `>>` are operators and also end a word. Check `>>` before `>`.
- 'single quotes' keep everything literally, backslashes included, up to the next '.
- "double quotes" keep spaces. Inside them a backslash escapes only `"` and `\`; any other backslash stays as a character.
- Outside quotes a backslash makes the next character literal. A backslash at the very end is an error.
- Quoted and unquoted pieces that touch join into one word: a"b c"\ d is the single word `ab c d`. A quoted empty string "" is a real, empty argument, which is why you track "in a word" separately from "word text is non-empty".
- An unterminated quote is an error, not a guess.

Then parse the tokens into commands: split on `|`; `< file` sets stdin; `> file` or `>> file` sets stdout and whether to append. Reject an empty command (a leading, doubled or trailing pipe) and an operator with no file after it. A quoted '|' is a word, not an operator. Return plain dicts; executing comes in stage 3.

Misconception: “split on spaces, then strip the quotes.” It breaks the moment a quoted argument contains a space or a pipe.
Counterexample: echo "a | b" must be one command with the argument `a | b`.

You may compare with Python's shlex.split, which follows the same quoting rules this lesson uses, but your tokenizer must not call it. The hidden checks use shlex as an independent oracle on thousands of random lines.

Guided activity A: tokenize a"b c"\ d and echo a\b "q\"x\y" by hand. Guided activity B: parse sort < data.txt | uniq -c >> counts.txt into two command dicts.
On your own: write a test with a quoted operator and an empty argument before running the hidden checks.

stages.title: 2 · Run a process, and know what must be a built-in
stages.goal: Run external programs with an argument list, cwd and environment, and implement cd/export/exit as built-ins with shell-style statuses.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Stage 1; subprocess.run; os.path; what a process, cwd and environment variable are.

Every external command runs as a separate child process. The child gets a copy of the shell's current directory and environment, and it can change its own copy, never yours. That single fact decides what a shell must do itself:
- cd must be a built-in. A child process that changes directory dies with that change; the shell's own cwd never moves. Your shell keeps its cwd in a ShellState and passes it to every child (cwd=state.cwd).
- export must be a built-in, for the same reason: update state.env and pass env=state.env to children. Names start with a letter or _, then letters, digits or _.
- exit marks the shell as finished with a status; with no argument it reuses the last status.

Pass the argument list straight to subprocess.run with shell=False. The words from stage 1 reach the program exactly as parsed, with no second round of interpretation. That is the defence against an argument like `; rm -rf ~` being run as code.

Statuses are the shell's return values: 0 means success, anything else is a failure code chosen by the program. Shells use 127 for “command not found” and 126 for “found but not executable”, so produce those instead of crashing. Record the last status in state.status, which is what $? reports in a real shell. cd to a missing directory prints a message and returns 1, leaving the cwd unchanged.

Misconception: “I'll run cd through subprocess like everything else.” The check below starts a child that changes directory and shows your shell's cwd is untouched.

stages.title: 3 · Real pipes and redirects
stages.goal: Run every pipeline stage at once, connected by OS pipes, with < > >> redirects relative to the shell cwd.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Stages 1–2; file objects; subprocess.Popen; what end-of-file means for a reader.

The Terminal Lab passes text from one command to the next after each finishes. A real shell starts every stage at once and connects them with OS pipes: stage 1's stdout is stage 2's stdin, and data flows while both run. Three consequences:
1. Speed and memory: three stages that each take a second finish in about one second, not three, and a gigabyte can stream through without being held in memory.
2. End-of-file: a reader sees EOF only when every copy of the pipe's write end is closed. Popen gives the child its own copy, so after starting the next stage your shell must close its own copy of the previous pipe. Forget, and a reader that waits for EOF hangs.
3. Early exit: if a later stage quits early (like head), the producer's next write fails with a broken pipe and it stops. That only happens if no one else, your shell included, still holds the read end. Keeping your copy open makes the producer block once the pipe buffer (often 64 KiB) fills. This is the most common pipeline hang, and a hidden check times it.

Redirects replace a stage's stdin or stdout with a file, opened relative to state.cwd (not your Python process's cwd): `<` reads, `>` truncates, `>>` appends. A redirected stdout isn't piped onward, so the next stage gets no input from it. Wait for every process, return all statuses, and set state.status to the last stage's status, which is what POSIX shells report by default. A missing program in the middle gets status 127, and the stages around it still finish. Its upstream neighbour may then hit a broken pipe, because nobody reads its output, so that stage's status depends on timing, exactly as in a real shell. Don't write tests that assume it.

Misconception: “subprocess.run each stage and feed the output forward is the same thing.” It gives the same text for small inputs, but it runs stages one after another, holds everything in memory and can't stop early.

stages.title: 4 · A mini Git object store that real Git can read
stages.goal: Store blobs, trees and commits in Git's own object format, move refs safely, and walk history.
stages.lesson:
Prerequisites: Stages 1–3 (for the demo shell); bytes vs str; hashlib; zlib. Git Lab lessons 1–4 recommended.

The Git Lab showed history as snapshots and branches as movable labels. Underneath, Git is a content-addressed store: every object is saved under the hash of its own bytes, so the same content always has the same id, and any change makes a new id.

Git's object format, which you'll match byte for byte:
- Header: kind, a space, the payload length in decimal, then a NUL byte. id = SHA-1(header + payload) as 40 hex characters. Store zlib-compressed bytes at objects/<first 2 hex>/<remaining 38>.
- blob: the file's bytes. b'hello\n' must give ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a, which is what `git hash-object` prints.
- tree (flat, files only here): for each name in sorted order, b'100644 ' + name + b'\0' + the 20 raw bytes of the blob id (not hex).
- commit: lines `tree <id>`, one `parent <id>` per parent, `author <name> <email> <unix time> <tz>`, the same committer line, a blank line, the message, and a final newline.
Get any byte wrong (unsorted names, hex instead of raw bytes, a missing length) and your ids stop matching Git's. The visible check compares against ids produced by real Git.

Reading an object back, recompute its hash and refuse if it doesn't match: content addressing is what lets Git detect corruption. Objects never change; refs are small files naming a commit. Moving a ref safely is compare-and-swap: update it only if it still holds the value you read, otherwise refuse, because someone else moved it. Real Git does the same check when you push.

Misconception: “changing one file rewrites the whole history.” It changes that file's blob, the tree and the new commit. The other file's blob id is identical, and old commits are untouched.

Guided activity A: hash b'hello\n' by hand-assembling the header, and compare. Guided activity B: commit {a.txt, b.txt}, change b.txt, commit again, and list which ids changed.
On your own: the hidden checks tamper with a stored object and race two ref updates. Stretch: if git is installed, copy your objects into a fresh repository's .git/objects and run `git fsck --strict` and `git cat-file -p <id>`.

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:

    t1 = g.write_tree({'notes': b'tide\n', 'crew': b'ada\n'}); c1 = g.commit(t1, [], 'one', who)
    t2 = g.write_tree({'notes': b'tide\n', 'crew': b'ada, kofi\n'}); c2 = g.commit(t2, [c1], 'two', who)
    blob = lambda tree, name: g.get(tree)[1].split(name.encode() + b'\0', 1)[1][:20].hex()
    assert blob(t1, 'notes') == blob(t2, 'notes') and blob(t1, 'crew') != blob(t2, 'crew') and t1 != t2
    assert g.put('blob', b'tide\n') == blob(t1, 'notes') and g.write_tree({'crew': b'ada\n', 'notes': b'tide\n'}) == t1
    g.update_ref('main', c1, None); g.update_ref('main', c2, c1)
    assert g.log('main') == [c2, c1] and g.get(c2)[0] == 'commit' and b'parent ' + c1.encode() in g.get(c2)[1]
    lone = g.commit(t2, [], 'parent ' + c1, who)  # a message line that looks like a header
    g.update_ref('side', lone, None)
    assert g.log('side') == [lone], 'parents come from the headers, not the message'
